raw_plan.interpretation: I interpret this as one acquisition email brief for the dossier-qualified slice of the selected audience: national and devolved government digital teams. The relationship is unknown, so the email must introduce Plausible without assuming the reader uses Google Analytics, has a consent banner, or is already planning a migration. Its purpose is to earn a concrete product evaluation, not a sale or onboarding action.

intent.reason_now: Public-sector analytics choices are assessed for cookies, collection of identifiable visitor data, data residency and suitability for Information Governance or DPIA review.
intent.desired_action: Start a 30-day free trial to assess Plausible against the team's analytics and privacy requirements.

raw_plan.reader: A national or devolved government digital team assessing whether web analytics can provide useful traffic and behaviour data without cookies or identifiable visitor data.
raw_plan.reader_segment: An EU or UK public sector web team that must publish analytics without a consent banner
raw_plan.reader_profile_override: Product-aware public-sector digital professionals who need checkable implementation details suitable for an Information Governance or DPIA assessment.
raw_plan.reader_scope: National and devolved government digital teams only; do not generalize the fit to every EU or UK public-sector web team.
raw_plan.promise: Give national and devolved government digital teams a concrete basis for evaluating web analytics that uses no cookies, collects no identifiable visitor data and processes visitor data only in the EU.
raw_plan.orientation: Plausible is hosted web analytics whose documentation states that it uses no cookies, collects no personal data about visitors and processes visitor data only on EU servers—the material an Information Governance or DPIA review must assess.
raw_plan.arc: In one email, move from the audience's assessment criteria to Plausible's documented privacy mechanism, then invite the team to test whether the product also meets its practical analytics needs.
raw_plan.sequence_rationale: Because the contract requires one acquisition email, the email must stand alone. It should lead with the audience's evaluation criteria, supply specific mechanism-level evidence rather than a broad compliance claim, and end with one product-evaluation step. It must not depend on an assumed incumbent, migration project or prior contact.

emails.selection_reason: The no-cookie, no-identifiable-personal-data design directly addresses the privacy and governance questions this audience must assess. A trial lets the team determine whether the resulting analytics are useful enough for its own reporting requirements.
emails.job: Earn a 30-day product evaluation against the team's analytics, Information Governance and DPIA requirements.
emails.single_idea: Plausible is worth evaluating when a government digital team needs useful web analytics without cookies or identifiable visitor data, backed by a documented anonymisation mechanism and EU-only processing.
emails.status_quo: Public-sector analytics choices can require an Information Governance or DPIA review covering cookies, visitor-data collection and where that data is processed.
emails.mechanism: Plausible uses no cookies. It derives a daily changing identifier by hashing the visitor's IP address and User-Agent with a rotating salt, rather than storing those raw values, and processes visitor data exclusively on servers owned and operated by European companies within the EU.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: Government digital teams may also need to publish performance data or give colleagues controlled access. Plausible provides documented sharing choices that can be evaluated directly during a trial.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: Plausible is worth evaluating as a way to share or publish web-performance data without handing every stakeholder the same level of dashboard access.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: Plausible lets a team invite users, assign permissions, create shared links, configure email reports or make a dashboard public.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: evaluating another analytics product may appear unrelated to the team's performance-publication workflow. After: the team sees a specific set of sharing controls it can test against that workflow.
must_not_say: Do not claim these controls satisfy a statutory publication standard.
Do not claim dashboards hide sensitive information by default.
Do not claim every public-sector team currently shares logins or lacks publication tooling.
Do not add privacy, migration, pricing or reporting-depth claims to this alternative argument.
alternative_arguments.call_to_action: Start a 30-day free trial and test the sharing options with a representative reporting workflow.
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Decide whether Plausible's permissions, shared links, reports and public-dashboard option fit the team's approach to internal access and published performance data.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The trial lets the team inspect the documented sharing options in the product against a representative reporting workflow.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: This test does not establish compliance with the team's publication policy, accessibility requirements or approval process.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Lead with the practical decision about sharing or publishing performance data, not a generic collaboration claim.

emails.belief_shift: Before: a privacy-friendly analytics claim may sound too general to support a public-sector assessment. After: Plausible presents specific, checkable design and residency details that justify a practical evaluation.
must_not_say: Do not claim Plausible guarantees GDPR, CCPA or other legal compliance.
Do not claim that every implementation is legally exempt from consent requirements.
Do not tell the reader to remove an existing consent banner.
Do not assume the reader currently uses Google Analytics, GA4, BigQuery, Looker Studio or any other named tool.
Do not claim full feature parity with Google Analytics or another platform.

Do not claim the trial completes an Information Governance, DPIA, security or procurement review.
Do not introduce pricing, customer logos, uptime, raw-data exports, APIs, funnels or other secondary features.

emails.objection: Our Information Governance or DPIA review needs implementation details, not a general privacy claim.
emails.call_to_action: Start a 30-day free trial and evaluate Plausible against one representative public-service website and reporting requirement.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether Plausible's analytics are useful enough, under its documented privacy model, to advance to the team's formal governance and procurement review.
emails.next_step_value: The trial gives the team a concrete environment in which to assess the product while checking its no-cookie design, anonymisation mechanism and EU-only processing against internal requirements.
emails.next_step_limit: A trial does not provide legal approval, complete a DPIA or procurement review, or establish that an existing analytics stack can be retired.

events.subject: Evaluate analytics without cookies
events.preview_text: Test Plausible against one public-service website and reporting requirement.
events.body:
Evaluate Plausible Analytics on one representative public-service website and compare its reporting with a requirement your team needs to meet.

Plausible is hosted web analytics that uses no cookies and collects no personal data about visitors. Its documented design provides specific implementation details for an Information Governance or DPIA assessment.

A daily changing identifier is created by hashing the visitor’s IP address and User-Agent with a rotating salt. The salt is rotated and deleted every 24 hours, while the raw IP address and User-Agent are never written to disk.

All visitor data is processed exclusively on servers owned and operated by European companies and never leaves the EU.

The 30-day trial gives your team a working environment to assess whether the analytics are useful enough, under this privacy model, to advance to formal governance and procurement review.

events.message: Email 1, draft 1: "Control access to performance data"
events.subject: Control access to performance data
events.preview_text: Test permissions, shared links, email reports and public dashboards in one reporting workflow.
events.body:
Sharing performance data does not have to mean giving every stakeholder the same dashboard access. Plausible lets teams invite users and assign permissions, then create shared links, configure email reports or make a dashboard public.

Plausible Analytics is hosted web analytics software with several ways to control how website data is shared. Those options can support distinct routes for internal access and published performance data.

A 30-day trial provides a practical way to inspect these controls in the product. Use a representative reporting workflow to see which permissions colleagues need, what a shared link exposes and whether an email report or public dashboard suits the intended audience.

The result is a concrete basis for deciding whether Plausible fits the team’s access and publication approach.

events.summary: A hosted web analytics service that would let our team manage access to performance data and distribute it through shared links, email reports or public dashboards.
issues: Rewrite "Plausible Analytics is hosted web analytics software with several ways to control how website data is shared." to state whether the service can operate without non-essential cookies or a consent banner, if supported, and point to the relevant privacy and data-handling documentation.

Rewrite "Those options can support distinct routes for internal access and published performance data." to specify what a public-sector team can expose publicly versus keep restricted, without implying that these routes meet governance requirements automatically.

Replace "A 30-day trial provides a practical way to inspect these controls in the product." with a lower-effort first step: review concrete documentation on cookie use, data processing, hosting, security and public-dashboard exposure before asking the team to configure a trial.

Cut or make specific "The result is a concrete basis for deciding whether Plausible fits the team’s access and publication approach." The trial described tests sharing controls, but not the defining consent and governance requirements.
events.biggest_doubt: I cannot tell whether this service can collect the analytics we need without non-essential cookies or a consent banner, and whether it supplies the privacy, data-handling and governance information a public-sector review would require. I would not begin a trial before establishing that basic eligibility.
events.stopped_at: A 30-day trial provides a practical way to inspect these controls in the product.
